desc:
Return the largest difference between two adjacent elements of nums once it has been sorted in ascending order. If the array has fewer than two elements, return 0.

Try to solve it in linear time and space, without a comparison sort.

For example, [3, 6, 9, 1] sorts to [1, 3, 6, 9], so the answer is 3.
hints: Sorting and scanning neighbours is O(n log n). The question is how to find the largest gap without ordering everything.
With n numbers between min and max, the n - 1 gaps sum to max - min, so the largest gap is at least ceil((max - min) / (n - 1)).

Use buckets of width w = max(1, (max - min) // (n - 1)). Two numbers inside one bucket differ by less than w, so the maximum gap never lies inside a bucket. Store only the min and max of each bucket and compare each bucket's min with the previous non-empty bucket's max.
editorial: Let lo and hi be the minimum and maximum. If lo == hi the answer is 0. Otherwise choose the bucket width w = max(1, (hi - lo) // (n - 1)) and put every number x into bucket (x - lo) // w. By the pigeonhole principle the best gap is at least the average gap, which is at least w, while any two numbers in the same bucket differ by at most w - 1. So the winner is always a gap between two buckets.

For every bucket keep only its smallest and largest value. Sweep the buckets in index order and for each non-empty one compute its min - max of the previous non-empty bucket; the maximum of these is the answer. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, because there are at most n buckets. This is the pigeonhole form of bucket sort, and it never needs to sort inside a bucket.
